title: How Are You?
outcomes: Ask someone how they are in formal and informal Spanish
Respond with at least four different answers about how you feel
Use ¿Y tú? / ¿Y usted? to return the question politely

sections.content: Now that you can greet people, the natural next step is asking how they're doing. This is the glue of every conversation — and at Kwik Trip, it turns a quick transaction into a real human moment. You'll learn how to ask, how to answer, and how to bounce the question back.

items: Ask someone how they are in formal and informal Spanish
Respond with at least four different answers about how you feel
Use ¿Y tú? / ¿Y usted? to return the question politely

items.notes: Use with friends, coworkers your age
Sounds like English — easy to remember
Polite — use this at work with customers

sections.heading: Micro Grammar — Estar (to be)
sections.content: Spanish has two verbs that mean "to be": ser and estar. For now, you only need estar — it's the one used for feelings and temporary states. ¿Cómo estás? literally means "How are you (right now)?" The difference between estás and está is just formality: estás = tú (informal), está = usted (formal). At Kwik Trip, default to ¿Cómo está? with customers. With coworkers you're close with, ¿Cómo estás? is fine.

sections.heading: Core Dialogue
sections.context: Afternoon shift at Kwik Trip — a regular Spanish-speaking customer comes to the register

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Hello! Good afternoon. How are you?

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.english: Good, thanks. And you?

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Very good, thanks for asking.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.english: I'm glad.

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Anything else?

breakdown.explanation: How are you? (formal) — You used the polite form with a customer. Perfect for work.
Thanks for asking — A warm phrase that shows you appreciate the conversation.
I'm glad — A common, friendly response when someone says they're doing well.
Anything else? — A handy register phrase you'll use constantly. Preview of future lessons!

questions.question: Which form did the employee use to ask 'How are you?' — and why?
options: Informal (estás) — because the customer is young
Formal (está) — because they're speaking to a customer

questions.question: What does 'más o menos' mean?
When should you use '¿Y usted?' instead of '¿Y tú?'

sections.heading: Guided Practice
sections.prompt: A customer just greeted you. Ask them how they are (formally).
sections.hint: Use the formal form of estar...
sections.feedback: ¡Muy bien! ¿Cómo está? is polite, professional, and shows you care.

turns.prompt: Your coworker says: "¡Hola! ¿Cómo estás?" — Tell them you're doing so-so.
They say: "¿Qué pasó?" (What happened?) — Say you're okay and ask how they are (informal).
turns.hint: Say good/well, then bounce it back with 'and you?'

turns.prompt: A customer greets you: "Buenas tardes." — Greet them back and ask how they are formally.

questions.question: Which answer means 'so-so'?
Fill in the blank: ¿Cómo ___? (formal 'How are you?')
You're at the register with a customer. Which is the safest way to ask how they are?
A customer asks '¿Cómo está?' — You're doing great. Reply: '______, gracias.'

sections.heading: Real-World Scenario
sections.content: At Kwik Trip, many regulars come in daily. Adding '¿Cómo está?' after your greeting transforms the interaction — it shows you see them as a person, not just a transaction. You don't need to understand every word of their response. If you hear 'bien,' smile and nod. If you hear 'mal' or they look down, a simple 'Lo siento' (I'm sorry) goes a long way. The goal isn't perfect Spanish — it's genuine connection.

sections.heading: Lesson Recap
points: ¿Cómo está? (formal) is your go-to at work — safe, polite, professional
¿Cómo estás? (informal) is for coworkers and friends
You know four responses: bien, muy bien, mal, más o menos, and regular
¿Y usted? bounces the question back formally — great customer service move
Even a simple '¿Cómo está?' can make a customer's day

title: What Is This?
outcomes: Ask what something is using ¿Qué es esto? and ¿Qué es eso?
Understand the difference between esto, eso, and aquel
Identify common store items in Spanish

sections.content: Customers point at things all the time — at the hot food counter, the drink station, the shelves. Knowing how to ask and answer 'What is this?' unlocks a huge chunk of real conversation. You'll learn demonstratives (this, that, that over there) and some common item names you'll actually use at Kwik Trip.

items: Ask what something is using ¿Qué es esto? and ¿Qué es eso?
Understand the difference between esto, eso, and aquel
Identify common store items in Spanish

items.notes: For something right here, near you
For something near the other person
For something far from both of you
Use to identify something close to you
Use to identify something near them
Masculine article even though it ends in -a

sections.heading: Micro Grammar — Demonstratives
sections.content: Spanish has three levels of distance for 'this/that': esto (this — near me), eso (that — near you), and aquello (that over there — far from both of us). When they stand alone as pronouns (not describing a noun), they end in -o and have no accent mark: esto, eso, aquello. You'll mostly use esto and eso at work. A customer pointing at the hot case? They'll say eso. You holding up a cup? Say esto. It maps perfectly to physical distance.

sections.heading: Core Dialogue
sections.context: A customer is at the Kwik Trip hot food counter pointing at items behind the glass

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.english: Excuse me, what is that?

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: That is pizza.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.english: And this?

lines.speaker: You
lines.spanish: Esto es un tornillo. Es como pan con jamón.
lines.english: This is a tornado. It's like bread with ham.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.spanish: Ah, muy bien. Quiero eso, por favor.
lines.english: Ah, very good. I want that, please.

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Of course! Here you go.

breakdown.explanation: What is that? — The customer is pointing at something behind the glass, near you. From their perspective, it's eso (near the other person).
This is a tornado (roller item). You're holding it, so it's esto (near me). Tornillo is a playful Spanglish term some use for the Kwik Trip tornado snack.
I want that — Quiero = I want. Eso = that. Simple and direct.
Here you go — Literally: 'Here you have.' A standard phrase when handing something to a customer.

questions.question: Why does the customer say 'eso' when pointing at the pizza?
options: Because it's far away from everyone
Because it's near the employee, not the customer

questions.question: What does '¿Qué es esto?' mean?
Which demonstrative would you use for something across the store?

sections.heading: Guided Practice
sections.prompt: A customer points at an item near you and asks what it is. The item is coffee. How do you respond?
sections.feedback: ¡Perfecto! Esto es café. Clear, simple, helpful.

turns.prompt: A customer points at something behind you and says: "¿Qué es eso?" — It's bread. Tell them.
They point to something right next to them and ask: "¿Y esto?" — It's milk. Answer them.
Now YOU want to ask what something far away is. Ask: 'What is that over there?'

questions.question: A customer holds up a bag and asks you what it is. They say:
Point at something near you and identify it: '_____ es café.'
How do you say 'the milk' in Spanish?
Translate: 'What is that?' (something near the other person)

sections.heading: Real-World Scenario
sections.content: At Kwik Trip, customers often point at items in the hot case, the bakery shelf, or the drink station without knowing the English names. If you can say 'Esto es pizza' or 'Eso es café,' you've just saved them from an awkward guessing game. You don't need to know every product name — start with the big ones: café, leche, agua, pan, pizza. When you don't know the Spanish word, just point and say 'Esto es...' followed by the English word. Most people will understand, and they'll appreciate that you tried.

sections.heading: Lesson Recap
points: ¿Qué es esto? = What is this? (near me) — use when holding something
¿Qué es eso? = What is that? (near you) — use when pointing at something near the other person
¿Qué es aquello? = What is that over there? — for distant items
You learned key store items: café, leche, agua, pan, pizza, dulces, papas fritas
Aquí tiene = Here you go — perfect for handing items to customers

title: Where Is...?
outcomes: Ask where something is located using ¿Dónde está?
Give simple directions using basic prepositions
Name common store locations customers ask about

sections.content: This might be the single most useful question you learn for work. Customers ask where things are constantly — the bathroom, the milk, the coffee, the ATM. After this lesson, you'll understand the question AND be able to point them in the right direction with basic Spanish.

items: Ask where something is located using ¿Dónde está?
Give simple directions using basic prepositions
Name common store locations customers ask about

items.notes: The big one — you'll hear this daily
Point and say this — works great

sections.heading: Micro Grammar — ¿Dónde está? vs. ¿Dónde están?
sections.content: You already know está from ¿Cómo está? — now you're using it for location. ¿Dónde está? = Where is (one thing)? ¿Dónde están? = Where are (multiple things)? For now, most questions will use está (singular). The accent on Dónde is critical — without it, donde means 'where' as a statement, not a question. In speech, you'll hear the rising question tone naturally.

sections.heading: Core Dialogue
sections.context: A customer approaches you at Kwik Trip looking confused

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.english: Excuse me, where is the bathroom?

lines.speaker: You
lines.spanish: Está al fondo, a la derecha.
lines.english: It's in the back, to the right.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.english: Thanks. And where is the milk?

lines.speaker: You
lines.spanish: La leche está allá, a la izquierda.
lines.english: The milk is over there, to the left.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.english: Thank you very much.

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: You're welcome. My pleasure.

breakdown.explanation: Where is the bathroom? — The single most common question you'll hear from Spanish-speaking customers. Memorize this one cold.

breakdown.phrase: Está al fondo, a la derecha
breakdown.explanation: It's in the back, to the right — Two directions chained together. Al fondo = in the back. A la derecha = to the right.
The milk is over there — You can put the item name first for clarity, then está + location.
My pleasure — A warm Latin American alternative to 'de nada.' Very common in Mexican Spanish.

questions.question: Where did the employee say the bathroom is?
options: In the back, to the right

questions.question: What does 'al fondo' mean?
How do you say 'to the left' in Spanish?

sections.heading: Guided Practice
sections.prompt: A customer asks: '¿Dónde está el baño?' — The bathroom is in the back. How do you respond?
acceptableAnswers: está al fondo, a la derecha
sections.feedback: ¡Excelente! 'Está al fondo' is clear and helpful. You can always point while you say it too.

turns.prompt: A customer walks up and says: "Disculpe, ¿dónde está el café?" — The coffee is over there, to the right. Tell them.
acceptableAnswers: el café está allá, a la derecha

turns.prompt: They then ask: "¿Y la salida?" — The exit is to the left. Respond.
acceptableAnswers: la salida está a la izquierda

turns.prompt: They say: "Muchas gracias." — Say 'You're welcome. My pleasure.'

questions.question: A customer asks '¿Dónde está el baño?' — What are they looking for?
Complete: El baño está ______ (in the back).
How do you say 'to the right'?
Translate: 'Where is the milk?'

sections.heading: Real-World Scenario
sections.content: At Kwik Trip, the top three things customers ask for in any language: bathroom, coffee, and specific products. If someone approaches you looking lost and says '¿Dónde está...?' followed by ANY word, your best move is to listen for that last word (the thing they want), then point and say 'Allá' (over there) or 'Al fondo' (in the back). Pointing plus one Spanish word beats a perfect sentence every time. As you get more comfortable, add the prepositions: 'Allá, a la derecha.' Baby steps.

phrases.spanish: Está al fondo, a la derecha.
phrases.english: It's in the back, to the right.

sections.heading: Lesson Recap
points: ¿Dónde está...? = Where is...? — your most practical question at work
El baño, la leche, el café, la salida, la caja — key store locations
Allá = over there, aquí = here — point and say these
A la derecha = right, a la izquierda = left, al fondo = in the back
Con gusto = My pleasure — a warm, Mexican-style 'you're welcome'

title: How Much Does It Cost?
outcomes: Ask how much something costs using ¿Cuánto cuesta?
Understand basic prices in Spanish with a number preview
Handle simple shopping interactions at the register

sections.content: Money talk is unavoidable at a store. Customers will ask about prices, and you'll need to understand (or at least catch) the numbers. This lesson gives you the question '¿Cuánto cuesta?' and a practical preview of numbers so you can handle basic price conversations without freezing up.

items: Ask how much something costs using ¿Cuánto cuesta?
Understand basic prices in Spanish with a number preview
Handle simple shopping interactions at the register

sections.heading: Micro Grammar — Cuesta vs. Cuestan
sections.content: Cuesta is for one item: ¿Cuánto cuesta la pizza? (How much does the pizza cost?) Cuestan is for multiple items: ¿Cuánto cuestan las papas fritas? (How much do the chips cost?) The verb cuesta/cuestan comes from 'costar' (to cost). You don't need to conjugate it beyond these two forms for now. Just remember: one thing = cuesta, many things = cuestan.

sections.heading: Core Dialogue
sections.context: A customer at Kwik Trip picks up a drink and some snacks and comes to the register

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.english: How much does this cost?

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: It costs two dollars and fifty cents.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.english: And this? Is it on sale?

lines.speaker: You
lines.spanish: Sí, está en oferta. Cuesta un dólar.
lines.english: Yes, it's on sale. It costs one dollar.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.spanish: Muy bien. Los dos, por favor.
lines.english: Very good. Both, please.

lines.speaker: You
lines.spanish: El total es tres dólares con cincuenta.
lines.english: The total is three dollars and fifty cents.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.english: Here you go. Five dollars.

lines.speaker: You
lines.spanish: Su cambio: un dólar con cincuenta. ¡Gracias!
lines.english: Your change: one dollar and fifty cents. Thanks!

breakdown.explanation: How much does this cost? — Esto because the customer is holding the item.
Two dollars and fifty cents — 'Con' (with) connects dollars and cents. Think: 'two dollars WITH fifty.'
It's on sale — Estar + en oferta. Great for pointing out deals to customers.
Your change — Su = your (formal). Cambio = change (money returned).

questions.question: How much was the item on sale?
What does 'con' mean in 'dos dólares con cincuenta'?
What is 'el cambio'?

sections.heading: Guided Practice
sections.prompt: A customer holds up a coffee and asks how much. It costs three dollars. How do you say it?
sections.feedback: ¡Muy bien! Cuesta tres dólares. Short, clear, and exactly what the customer needs to hear.

turns.prompt: A customer points at chips and asks: "¿Cuánto cuesta?" — They cost two dollars. Tell them.
They ask: "¿Está en oferta?" — Yes, it's on sale. Confirm it.
The total is five dollars. They hand you ten. Give their change: "Your change is five dollars."

questions.question: How do you ask 'How much does this cost?'
Fill in the blank: La pizza _______ cinco dólares. (costs)
How do you say 'It's on sale'?
Translate: 'Your change is two dollars.'

sections.heading: Real-World Scenario
sections.content: At the Kwik Trip register, prices are on the screen, but customers sometimes ask before they get there — especially at the hot food counter or the drink station. You don't need to memorize every number right now (that comes in a future unit). For now, the survival strategy is: if a customer asks '¿Cuánto cuesta?' and you know the price, say the number + 'dólares.' If you don't know the price, point to the price tag or the register screen and say 'Aquí' (here). That's perfectly fine. The key numbers to know right now: uno (1), dos (2), tres (3), cinco (5), diez (10), veinte (20).

sections.heading: Lesson Recap
points: ¿Cuánto cuesta? = How much does it cost? — your key shopping phrase
Cuesta (one item) vs. cuestan (multiple items)
Number preview: uno, dos, tres, cinco, diez, veinte
Dos dólares con cincuenta = $2.50 — 'con' connects dollars and cents
Está en oferta = It's on sale, Su cambio = Your change, El total = The total

title: Can You Help Me?
outcomes: Ask for help politely using ¿Me puede ayudar?
Offer help to customers with ¿En qué le puedo ayudar?
Handle situations where you need to get a coworker or manager

sections.content: This is the lesson where everything comes together. Asking for help and offering help are two sides of the same coin — and at Kwik Trip, both happen constantly. You'll learn how to be the helpful employee AND how to ask when you're the one who needs a hand. This is real customer service Spanish.

items: Ask for help politely using ¿Me puede ayudar?
Offer help to customers with ¿En qué le puedo ayudar?
Handle situations where you need to get a coworker or manager

items.notes: Formal — great for asking customers or managers
THE customer service phrase — memorize this one
Warm way to say you're happy to help

sections.heading: Micro Grammar — Poder (can / to be able to)
sections.content: Poder means 'can' or 'to be able to.' You'll use two forms: puedo (I can) and puede (you can / he-she can). ¿Me puede ayudar? = Can you help me? (Literally: Can-you me help?) ¿En qué le puedo ayudar? = How can I help you? (Literally: In what you can-I help?) Notice the word order is different from English — the object pronoun (me, le) goes before the verb. Don't overthink it. Just memorize these as fixed phrases for now.

sections.heading: Core Dialogue
sections.context: A customer walks into Kwik Trip looking confused, holding a piece of paper

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Hello! How can I help you?

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.spanish: Sí, necesito encontrar la leche de almendras.
lines.english: Yes, I need to find the almond milk.

lines.speaker: You
lines.spanish: Un momento, por favor... La leche está allá, al fondo.
lines.english: One moment, please... The milk is over there, in the back.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.english: Can you help me find it?

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Of course! Come with me.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.english: Thank you very much for your help.

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: With great pleasure. Do you need anything else?

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.english: No, thanks. That's everything.

breakdown.explanation: How can I help you? — Your #1 customer service opener. 'Le' = you (formal object pronoun). Practice this until it's automatic.
One moment, please — Buys you time to think. Use it whenever you need a second to process.
Of course! — Stronger than just 'sí.' Shows enthusiasm and willingness to help.
Come with me — Venga = come (formal command). Conmigo = with me. Use this to walk customers to what they need.
Do you need anything else? — Perfect closing question. Algo más = something more/anything else.
That's everything / That's all — The customer's way of saying they're done. You'll hear this often.

questions.question: What did the customer need help finding?
What does '¡Claro que sí!' mean?
What does 'Eso es todo' mean?

sections.heading: Guided Practice
sections.prompt: A customer walks in looking lost. Offer to help them using the standard customer service phrase.
acceptableAnswers: hola en qué le puedo ayudar
sections.feedback: ¡Perfecto! '¿En qué le puedo ayudar?' is the gold standard of customer service Spanish. Say it with a smile and you're golden.

turns.prompt: A customer approaches you at the register. Offer to help them.
turns.hint: How can I help you? OR Do you need help?

turns.prompt: The customer speaks too fast and you didn't catch it. Ask them to repeat more slowly.
turns.hint: Can you repeat? OR Slower, please...

turns.prompt: You still can't help — you need to get someone else. Tell them: 'One moment, I'm going to find someone.'
acceptableAnswers: un momento, voy a buscar a alguien
un momento por favor, voy a buscar a alguien
un momento. voy a buscar a alguien
turns.hint: One moment + I'm going to find someone...

questions.question: What is the standard way to offer help to a customer in Spanish?
You need help. Ask: 'Can you help me?'
A customer spoke too fast. What do you say?
You need to go get your manager. Say: 'One moment, please.'

sections.heading: Real-World Scenario
sections.content: Here's the truth about working at Kwik Trip with Spanish-speaking customers: you won't always understand everything. That's okay. The phrases in this lesson are your safety net. If a customer needs help, open with '¿En qué le puedo ayudar?' If they answer and you're lost, say '¿Puede repetir, por favor?' or 'Más despacio, por favor.' If you still can't figure it out, 'Un momento — voy a buscar a alguien' lets you tag in a bilingual coworker without anyone feeling embarrassed. The goal is never perfection. The goal is effort, warmth, and problem-solving.

sections.heading: Lesson Recap
points: ¿En qué le puedo ayudar? = How can I help you? — your customer service opener
¿Me puede ayudar? = Can you help me? — when YOU need help
¿Necesita ayuda? = Do you need help? — for customers who look lost
Safety phrases: Un momento, No entiendo, ¿Puede repetir?, Más despacio
Voy a buscar a alguien = I'm going to find someone — your graceful exit when you need backup
